bp: Software development is not just typing code into a file. A working engineering system starts with a need, turns that need into a specification, breaks it into tasks, writes changes, runs tests, finds mistakes, reviews risks, and finally connects the result to version control and deployment pipelines. This tutorial is about replacing simple code suggestion with agent teams that can participate in that whole loop. The real-world object is the development workflow itself: planning, coding, testing, reviewing, debugging, and shipping under human supervision. GitHub Copilot, Mistral Codec, and Kiro are used as examples of this shift. The paper matters because a single model that predicts the next piece of code is useful but incomplete. Real teams need repeatable assurance: Did the change satisfy the spec? Did tests fail? Did review catch a security problem? Did the agent remember relevant project context? The tutorial frames AI-assisted development as a coordinated engineering process rather than a fancy autocomplete box.
wh: The hard part is that software work creates consequences outside the sentence being written. A line of code may compile, but still violate the design goal, break a hidden dependency, expose private data, or fail after deployment. A coding agent therefore cannot be judged only by whether its immediate answer sounds plausible. It has to carry context across many steps, use tools correctly, and accept evidence from runtime feedback. The abstract points to several tensions: multi-agent coordination can help divide work, but the agents must not talk past one another; long-term memory can preserve project knowledge, but stale or irrelevant memory can mislead; tool-integrated verification can catch errors, but only if the right tests, review checks, and routes are chosen. Evaluation is hard because success is not one number. Reliability, security, cost, scalability, safe deployment, and integration with IDEs, version control, and CI/CD pipelines all matter at the same time.
naive: A smart beginner would start with a single powerful language model inside an editor and ask it to write the requested code. If the answer looks reasonable, the developer could paste it, run it, and fix whatever breaks. That is a useful first step, but it fails as an end-to-end workflow. The model sees only part of the project, so it may miss a design constraint or previous decision. It can generate code without knowing whether tests pass. It may not separate planning, implementation, review, and security checking. It also gives little structure for measuring whether the process is reliable or repeatable. The beginner approach treats software development as one response; the tutorial treats it as a loop of planned actions and checked evidence.
ap: The core idea is to organize language models as collaborating workers around a software lifecycle. Instead of one model producing one completion, the workflow assigns roles: one part can decompose a task, another can write code, another can run tools, another can inspect failures, and another can review safety or quality. A manager or routing layer decides which tool or role should act next. Spec-driven development gives the agents a shared target, so their work can be checked against something more concrete than a vague request. Reflection means the system looks back at its own output and feedback, such as a failed test or review comment, before trying again. Memory and context maintenance keep relevant project facts available across turns. The central move is therefore mechanical: close the loop from generation to assurance by making planning, coding, testing, reviewing, and deployment checks visible parts of the same agent workflow.
mech: The mechanism begins with a human engineering request or a specification. The first transformation is task decomposition: the system breaks the request into smaller work items that can be planned, implemented, and checked. Next, a coding role proposes changes using the available project context. That context may include the current files, earlier decisions, retrieved documentation, prior debugging traces, or memory of conventions. A manager-tool router then chooses concrete actions: use an IDE integration, inspect version-control state, run a test command, call a linter, search project history, or trigger a CI/CD check. The important point is that external tools return evidence, not just more text. A compiler error, failing unit test, review warning, or runtime trace becomes feedback that changes the next step. Reflective collaboration lets an agent compare the attempted change with the spec and the observed failure, then decide whether to revise code, ask for more information, or escalate risk to a human. Role-specialized teams can separate concerns: a planner keeps the task shape, an implementer edits, a debugger reasons from runtime feedback, and a reviewer looks for correctness or security guardrail failures. The output is not merely a code snippet. It is a proposed engineering change plus a record of checks that make the change more repeatable and easier to evaluate.
math: The main mathematical idea is controlled search through a large space of possible next actions. At each point the system has a goal, partial context, many possible tools, and uncertain evidence about what will work. Choosing the next step is a scoring problem: which action is most likely to reduce the remaining error relative to the spec while staying within cost, safety, and time limits? Task decomposition is a tree-like split of a large problem into smaller subproblems, where progress on leaves should add up to progress on the whole. Routing is a matching problem: compare the current need with the abilities of tools or agent roles, then send work to the closest fit. Verification is a comparison between intended behavior and observed behavior; tests and runtime traces turn vague correctness into concrete pass, fail, or warning signals. Memory and retrieval use similarity: past facts are useful only when the current task is close enough in project, file, API, or decision context. Reflection is iterative error reduction: observe what went wrong, change the plan or code, and check again. The tradeoffs are explicit: more agents can add coverage but also coordination cost; more memory can add context but also noise; stronger guardrails can prevent risky actions but slow development.
dots: This paper belongs with the repo's LLM Agents and Tool Use family, whose family writeup describes the shared problem as turning a language model from a talker into a worker that chooses tools, uses memory, and stops safely. It is also close to the conversational search tutorial in `data/rich_paper_out/161.json`, because both treat an interactive system as an ongoing decision loop rather than a one-shot answer. Neighboring input papers show the same pressure in other settings: MCP-Focus improves tool documentation so agents can select servers; Tool-Star trains web agents to coordinate multiple tools; AgentSim builds grounded traces for retrieval agents; production shopping agents must balance accuracy, latency, reliability, and cost; tool-invocation refusal studies when an agent should not call a tool. This tutorial applies that broader conference pattern to software development. The surface vocabulary is coding, but the deeper problem is controlled action under uncertainty with outside evidence and real deployment consequences.
ww: The approach works when it changes the source of confidence. A single code completion asks the reader to trust a plausible answer. A collaborative workflow asks the system to earn trust by exposing intermediate decisions and checking them against evidence. Decomposition helps because smaller tasks are easier to assign, inspect, and repair than a whole feature request. Role specialization helps when different failure modes require different attention: writing code, finding a runtime cause, checking security, and judging review quality are not the same activity. Tool routing helps because software projects already contain reliable instruments, such as tests, version control, IDE diagnostics, and CI checks. Runtime feedback is especially important because it turns hidden errors into observable signals that can drive another attempt. Spec-driven development gives the loop a target, so revision is not random tinkering. Memory helps when the same project conventions or earlier decisions repeatedly matter. The gain comes from making software generation less like guessing a final answer and more like running a monitored engineering process.
po: The payoff is a practical blueprint for designing and evaluating collaborative coding agents in real engineering environments. The tutorial promises concepts and live demonstrations around task decomposition, memory and retrieval, autonomous debugging with runtime feedback, and integration into IDEs, version control, and CI/CD pipelines. It also distills do-and-don't patterns for reliability, security, cost, and scalability. Because the abstract is for a tutorial, the result is not a reported accuracy number. The capability it buys is a clearer way to build agentic development systems whose outputs can be checked, reviewed, and deployed with measurable assurance rather than treated as isolated suggestions.
limits: The abstract is truncated at the end and does not provide a dataset, metric, controlled user study, or measured productivity result. It describes a tutorial and blueprint, so its claims depend on the quality of the synthesis and demonstrations. The approach assumes that the specification is clear enough to guide work, that project context can be retrieved without flooding the agent with irrelevant material, and that tests or review tools actually capture the important failures. Multi-agent coordination must add useful checks rather than extra disagreement. Safe deployment also requires security guardrails, human oversight, and evaluation that reflects real repositories, not only clean examples.
